https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cpd7.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Sulyok said he had no constitutional recourse to challenge the amendment By Nick Thorpe ,Â Reporting from Hungary Â and Â Henry Moore Published 18 July 2026 Hungarian President TamÃ¡s Sulyok has agreed to step down, signing an amendment to the country's constitution which will end his presidency at midnight on Sunday. Prime Minister PÃ©ter Magyar's Tisza party had steamrolled the law change through parliament to oust Sulyok - widely seen as a loyalist of former prime minister Viktor OrbÃ¡n who lost power in April after 16 years. Sulyok had five days to sign the amendment or risk a protracted constitutional crisis and impeachment proceedings. He confirmed he would agree to the law change as the deadline passed on Saturday evening, but in a statement accused Magyar's government of violating the rule of law. He said the amendment marked a "breaking point in Hungarian constitutional democracy" and said the "core values of a free society... have been trampled underfoot for the sake of political power". It marks the latest and most dramatic move by the Tisza government, which saw Sulyok as a puppet of the former government and had pushed for his resignation. It has swept through major constitutional changes since winning a landslide victory in April. The 17th amendment, passed with an overwhelming majority on Monday , ends the president's term citing "serious loss of confidence" in him. It also removes the head of the Constitutional Court and forbids MPs who have served three terms from standing again - which applies to more than half the current deputies from OrbÃ¡n's Fidesz party. OrbÃ¡n had described the amendment as an act of tyranny and called for protests. Since the April election, Fidesz has been in free fall, reeling from the shock defeat. OrbÃ¡n himself has hardly been seen in public, and refused to take his seat in parliament. Image source, EPA/Shutterstock Image caption, Since his party swept to power in April, PÃ©ter Magyar (left) has repeatedly called on Sulyok (right) to resign In office from 2010 until 2026, Fidesz reshaped the Hungarian state to its own will, and filled supposedly independent state positions with party loyalists using its own two-thirds majority. The 141 Tisza deputies in parliament gave a standing ovation as the results of the vote passing the amendment were announced on Monday. After the vote, AndrÃ¡s Baka, former head of Hungary's Supreme Court, told the BBC: "I quite agree with the removal of the president." Hungary was governed by the rule of law from 1989 to 2010, he argued, after which Fidesz captured state institutions and created an authoritarian state. "And it is now very difficult to break up a sophisticated authoritarian regime... which was designed to survive even after electoral defeat," Baka said. Photograph: Alexander Ermochenko/Reuters Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Ukraine war briefing: Nuclear plant has lost power and running on generators, UN watchdog says Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia plant has 10-day diesel supply on site; Kyiv investigates deadly attack on warehouse. What we know on day 1,649 Guardian staff and agencies Sat 29 Aug 2026 21.07 EDT Last modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 21.08 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant in Ukraine has been without off-site power for more than a week and is now relying on emergency diesel generators, the UN’s nuclear watchdog says. The plant, which needs power to keep its six non-operating reactors cool, has only a 10-day diesel supply on site, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said on Saturday. “The availability of diesel fuel is of paramount importance whenever a nuclear power plant loses off-site power, ” said agency director general Rafael Grossi. “The current situation once again shows why reliable external power and secure supply routes are indispensable for nuclear safety and security.” The plant had been supplied with diesel on Thursday and Friday from another off-site location, the IAEA added. Love under anti-drone nets: Ukrainian couple wed in Kramatorsk combat zone Read more Zaporizhzhia lost its regular power supply “following military activity on the northern side of the Dnipro River”, the statement said. The IAEA said it was trying to negotiate a local ceasefire to allow repairs to electrical lines. The plant, in southern Ukraine, was seized by the Russian army in March 2022 and its six reactors have been shut down since that year. Germany is reportedly preparing to blame Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport and impose sanctions on Russian entities . Friedrich Merz’s government is expected to announce the “extensive” measures in the next week, Politico reports , potentially alongside a new EU sanctions package. Ukrainian prosecutors have opened an investigation into why munitions were stored so close to homes after a deadly Russian attack on a warehouse storing “explosive objects” near Kyiv’s western suburbs. At least 37 people were killed in the attack on the warehouse in Myla on Friday, making it the war’s deadliest attack this year, Donna Ferguson reports . The attack damaged at least 50 residential buildings, including a care home for elderly and disabled people , and sparked a huge fire and explosions in the Bucha district of the Kyiv region. The regional governor, Tymur Tkachenko, said a further 42 people, including four children, had been injured in the strike. The warehouse was a depot owned by the Ukrainian military and stored shells, drones and other munitions , Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a video address. “The first impact was on a place where ammunition was being stored that absolutely should not have been there – a depot of the defence forces. [There was] detonation of shells, mines, other munitions and drones on a significant scale,” the Ukrainian president said. Finland’s president said he did not believe Russia would risk an attack against a ⁠Nato country , with Alexander Stubb telling the Bild newspaper that it would “make no sense” to test the resolve of the alliance. “I simply see neither evidence nor facts to support it,” ​he told Bild, adding that he ‌did not believe that Russia “would ever want to attack Nato, the world’s most powerful military ‌alliance”. Stubb, whose country joined Nato in 2023, said the alliance had to be prepared for any scenario but he did not believe Moscow was in a position to go to war with Nato. “It makes no sense ​for any power in the world to test the resolve of this alliance.” Russian drone strike on Kyiv warehouse storing weapons kills at least 37 Read more The ⁠Russian ​defence ministry said Russian troops had captured the ⁠village of Khrapivshchyna ​in ‌Ukraine’s Sumy ‌region , and the ‌villages of Novoandriivka and Rubizhne in the Donetsk region. The ministry ‌said on Saturday via its Telegram channel ​that it had struck a logistics centre in ⁠the Kyiv region ​where ​components for Ukrainian ​ballistic missiles ​were ‌stored. Reuters could ​not ​independently verify the report. Three people ⁠have ⁠been killed and ​nine ⁠injured in a ⁠Ukrainian ​drone ‌attack ‌in the ‌Russian Belgorod region , local authorities said ‌on their Telegram channel. Three ​of the ⁠injured were ​in a ​serious ​condition, ​ ‌officials said. Europe is ⁠making statements suggesting that it regards ⁠Russia as ⁠an “adversary ​and even an enemy,” Kremlin spokesperson ⁠Dmitry Peskov has claimed , adding that ⁠Moscow sees no ​prospect of ‌improved ‌relations between Russia and the ‌EU. It was not immediately clear which statements Peskov was referring to. Peskov added ‌that the EU’s current politicians are confrontational ​towards Russia, “not only in words but also in deeds”. In 2022, Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Since the conflict began, the UN in August had verified at least 16,874 civilians killed, including 820 children, and 51,173 injured, including 3,126 children. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c84g.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Hundreds of protesters continued to be detained in Delhi on Sunday By Geeta Pandey and Zoya Mateen Reporting from BBC Delhi Published 11 October 2026, 07:02 BST Updated 49 minutes ago India's Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has vowed to continue its protest seeking the resignation of top election official even as the city sees more demonstrations for a second day with thousands of security personnel deployed and roads barricaded. Abhijeet Dipke - who began the movement in May after India's Chief Justice likened some jobless young people to "cockroaches" - and other leaders were arrested on arrival in Delhi on Saturday. They were freed on Sunday. In his first comments after his release, Dipke said "the CJP will neither back down nor be intimidated". Media reports said, 7,000 protesters were detained and released on Saturday. Hundreds have also been detained on Sunday. The CJP - which is not registered as a political party in India - is seeking electoral reforms just months before crucial state elections. It has also demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating voters' lists - which the Election Commission has denied. On Sunday morning, Dipke and two other senior CJP leaders - Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka - were set free by a magistrate's court "on the condition that they will not engage in breach of peace for one year", police said. After his release, Dipke posted on X , external , saying: "Modi, as PM, is an embarrassment to India." In another post , external , he said he was going to his village to attend his grandmother's funeral who died around the time of his arrest yesterday. He added that "the CJP will neither back down nor be intimidated". Ranka and Das later told a press conference that the condition did not mean they couldn't protest. "Peaceful protest is our constitutional right and Jantar Mantar is a desginated protest site, so this doesn't mean we can't do peaceful protest," Ranka said. "Breach of peace is done by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Home Minister Amit Shah and CEC Gyanesh Kumar," he said, adding that the CJP will continue to protest. Saturday saw dramatic scenes as police officials boarded the flight to detain Dipke, Das and Ranka as their plane landed. Figure caption, 'Cockroach' leaders say they have been detained ahead of march For a second day in a row on Sunday, much of central Delhi had roads barricaded and offices, shops and restaurants shut and internet services curtailed. In Connaught Place, one of Delhi's busiest shopping and entertainment hubs, there are rows upon rows of bright yellow police barricades, guarded by thousands of police and paramilitary personnel. Protesters have returned to the area for a second consecutive day, but they are vastly outnumbered by security personnel and the BBC has witnessed many detentions. Some were put into buses before being driven away. Some could be seen peering through the windows, others trying to push their way out while shouting "Gyanesh must go!" At one point, an entire bus reverberated with similar chants. Every now and then, small groups of protesters managed to slip past the barricades and sprint through the streets, with police personnel chasing after them. Within moments, they were surrounded, detained and, in some instances, dragged across the road, before being bundled into waiting buses. The most dramatic moment came during the detention of activist Neha Bora , external who was chased by police personnel before being caught and detained. Some protesters also said they were feeling a little uncertain. One of them told the BBC that the absence of the CJP's top leadership on the ground was beginning to affect the movement's momentum. "Without them, we're feeling a little lost," the protester admitted, before quickly adding, "But that doesn't mean we'll stop our fight." Image caption, Security forces have been deployed across Delhi The CJP had called for a protest on Saturday at Jantar Mantar - the road that the demonstrators had occupied for weeks earlier this summer seeking education reforms. Police had refused them permission and the city was in a virtual lockdown with unprecedented curbs in place to thwart the protesters from reaching the venue. At least 45 metro stations were closed and Delhi's main railway stations were shut with major train services cancelled. Many protesters attempting to travel from outside were de-boarded en route. Internet was also curtailed in central Delhi for the entire day. After the police detained the CJP leaders and other activists, lawyers and students leaders, the CJP called for more protests on Sunday. On Sunday, the Indian Supreme Court held a special hearing to deal with complaints of shutdowns and detentions. The court ordered the government to restore internet and ensure that metro and rail services functioned normally, unless there was disturbance to public order. The court also said that free movement of people should be permitted and there should be no illegal detention. Figure caption, Watch: Why have hundreds of 'cockroach' protesters been detained in Delhi Why are people protesting? The row centres over a mammoth exercise to update electoral rolls nationwide - the commission has said it's a routine exercise to weed out dead, duplicate or ineligible voters. At least 130 million voter names have been purged from the rolls so far and in many states, the exercise has been shrouded in controversy, with tens of thousands of people alleging they have been wrongly removed. The CJP - and opposition parties - accuse Kumar of favouring Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in the way the electoral rolls are being updated. The Election Commission and the BJP have denied this. The CJP first emerged as a major protest movement during weeks of demonstrations over the summer demanding education reforms and the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. The group stemmed from a joke made by Dipke in response to a remark by Chief Justice Surya Kant, who had likened jobless youngsters to "cockroaches". He later said the comments were misinterpreted. Dipke, who previously worked with the opposition Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), had just completed a master's degree at Boston University when he posted a question on X in May: "What if all cockroaches come together?" The post went viral, and the CJP was born. Momentum built around the movement which tapped into anger over unemployment, exam paper leaks and government accountability. Their five-week-long protest ended in celebration for the protesters in July after the resignation of India's education minister. https://www.politico.eu/article/liz-trus.text: LONDON — Liz Truss claims the U.K. would have managed successful missions to Mars within years — if only her 49-day premiership hadn’t been cut short. The assertion comes in the former British prime minister’s new book “Bank Job,” which was published Monday and claims to explain “how the Bank of England broke the bond market and brought down the government” when her mini-budget in 2022 precipitated market turmoil. In its closing chapter, the book paints a vivid picture of what Truss believes life in 2040 would be like if her policies had been given a chance to bed in. “Several missions to Mars have now been launched from Britain’s space port,” Truss’ book imagines. Advertisement Advertisement The ex-PM also opts for some more grounded policy dreams. She envisages a 2040 in which “there are now no European Union laws in Britain,” a “permissive regime for artificial intelligence” is in place, and tumbling energy costs and faster planning timelines have helped make the U.K. a leader in AI. “Bitcoin received tax treatment consistent with its status as a form of money for commercial purposes,” she imagines. “No central bank digital currency was introduced.” Since leaving office after a revolt in her own party, Truss has dismissed claims her economic decisions — which included a huge energy bills bailout and tax cuts funded by fresh borrowing — were responsible for crashing the pound. She has instead pointed the finger at the central bank, the Treasury and the Office for Budget Responsibility watchdog, accusing them of working against her. Her new book takes direct aim at the Bank of England, which sold £80 billion of gilts the day before the mini-budget. Truss lost her House of Commons seat at the 2024 general election, and has since been involved in launching the Conservative Political Action Conference in Britain. Advertisement Advertisement
